title: The hate is caused by fear, and ironically, lack of talent.
author: GoGs0l0dev
selftext:
I made this profile because at the right time I’ll eventually start posting about my game.  It’s too rough yet, but I’ve been researching the community and trying to gain more insight.

So of course Reddit is like “oh you like AI, here’s more!”…and since Reddit is a horrible representation of the actual population, popular sentiment, etc. my home feed is now littered with anti AI subs and posts.

Sure they hate low effort, one shot “AI slop” games.  We all do.  I’m worried that the 100 low effort games in the same niche will make much harder no matter how many weeks and months I spend playtesting, iterating, QA/QC, etc.

But I think they are unintentionally exposing their biggest fear when they parrot “Well, for every one *decent* game, there’s 99 AI slop ones being made!”

They are terrified of that 1%.  They are terrified by games like Slotbound being successful.

The amount of people I see complaining while self-promoting their steam page for their “100% human made” is large…and a surprising amount of time, the game is shit.  The art style is atrocious, their steam trailers and screenshots look bad, the games seem shallow, and the list goes on.

They are terrified by the people who became laborers, blue collar/white collar, or didn’t enter CompSci being able to enter.  Scared shitless of lifelong gamers, with creativity and programmatic mindset, and who understand what their genre and niche needs, wants, or may be missing.

Because in those cases, maybe not a one shot, but an individual like that can spend a month worth of weekly pro sub usage limits on Codex or whatever they choose…and make a game that is deeper, looks better, and plays better than what they’ve worked years on.

comments.author: Relevant-Positive-48
comments.body:
I have 28 years of professional software engineering experience, 16 of them in the game industry.  I also have released multiple indie titles.

I don't know why you (and you're not alone) seem to think that someone who has a CS degree, learned how to code before AI, or works or has worked in the industry means they're uncreative, disconnected to what users want, lack an aesthetic sense, have no game design skills and are useless when it comes to business and marketing while people who have never been involved in CS have all of those things.

replies.author: GoGs0l0dev
replies.body:
It depends on the person.

What I’m calling out is some people code and don’t have any knack or natural or acquired gift for the overall holistic product.

And I’ve experienced that in my professional life as well as on reddit.

I work FAANG and in the last year I’ve transitioned to a role that is effectively front deployed engineer for Anthropic with a different title.  95% of my job is “vibe coding” enterprise and internal tooling that is replacing any 3rd party tooling with basically the exception being payroll stuff like Workday or financial stuff.

Gone are the days of me only being able to do basic sql and queries, and having to deal with BE engineers who have 15+ years experience and still struggle with basic UI/UX.  And that’s high paid, tech SWEs to boot.

It’s anecdotal, but it’s a large sample size.  Just like some senior/principal engineer that still has to rely on junior IC and PD teams to make all frontend decisions because they just aren’t good at it…I’ve seen plenty of coders on here complaining they have 47 wishlists for a game they spent 3 years developing and I see why.

It can look every bit as shitty as the posts on this sub that are check out this “game” I made in 4 hours.  The sad thing is they spend 36 months on it instead of 3.6 hours.

I’ll admit maybe a bit of ego is showing for me, if you can admit the same for yourself just because you have a degree in the space.

replies.author: Yo-Soy-Groot
replies.body: No one gives a shit that you work at a FAANG company.

replies.author: GoGs0l0dev
replies.body: It’s relevant to the point I’m trying to make, but clearly you feel a certain way about it sheesh.

replies.author: Yo-Soy-Groot
replies.body: Tell us all of your other made up credentials, please

replies.author: GoGs0l0dev
replies.body:
I’m not making it up.  Unfortunately, my RSUs are much smaller than real SWEs so I’m not making 800k plus total comp like other senior ICs that are traditional SWEs.

But you cry yourself to sleep knowing I clear 350k total comp a year and 95% of my day is voice to text talking to Claude and Codex and landing AI generated diffs while sitting at a desk.

You just come across as both jaded and narcissistic, even before AI a good game was made from a good Idea that was well executed now with AI some of the technical steps are much easier and quicker. I think anyone who focuses on how long something took at either end of the spectrum is putting to much importance on themselves over their game.

replies.author: Relevant-Positive-48
replies.body:
Sure, people tend to be good at certain things and not good at other things and some people are multi talented in more areas than other.  
  
This doesn't invalidate my point calling out a pattern that I see from many vibe coders in the video game space.  
  
They're, rightfully, thrilled that AI empowers them to unleash their creativity and implement their game ideas (that may have been developing and accumulating for a very long time) without needing to invest the many years it typically takes to master manual coding, the drive to build a team (via funding or excitement),  and then the years it would take to put a game together manually.  
  
But they also seem to think that people who did master manual coding can't also have great creativity and don't also benefit from the compressed timelines, and multidisciplinary output that other AI tools (image, video and sound generators for example), gives them.   
  
PS:  My ego is certainly involved here but not because I have a degree.  The pre-AI professional programmers I have worked who didn't have a degree were, invariably, among the best I've ever worked with.
